title: Min Stack — O(1) push/pop/top/getMin.
shortTitle: Min Stack — O(1) push, pop, top, and getMin

s1_definition.profdef: A Min Stack is a stack that supports the usual push, pop, and top operations plus a getMin operation that returns the current minimum element, all in constant time. The standard design keeps an auxiliary stack in parallel with the main stack so that the top of the auxiliary stack is always the minimum of the elements currently in the main stack.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India stacks deposit slips one on top of another, and the manager must instantly answer "what is the smallest deposit still in this pile right now." Alongside the real pile, a clerk keeps a shadow pile where each slip records the smallest amount seen up to that point. When a slip is removed from the real pile, the matching shadow slip is removed too, so the top of the shadow pile is always the current smallest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a second stack whose top always holds the minimum so far, pushing and popping it in lockstep with the main stack to get the minimum in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Min Stack is a stack that supports the usual push, pop, and top operations plus a getMin operation that returns the current minimum element, all in constant time. The standard design keeps an auxiliary stack in parallel with the main stack so that the top of the auxiliary stack is always the minimum of the elements currently in the main stack.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India stacks deposit slips one on top of another, and the manager must instantly answer "what is the smallest deposit still in this pile right now." Alongside the real pile, a clerk keeps a shadow pile where each slip records the smallest amount seen up to that point. When a slip is removed from the real pile, the matching shadow slip is removed too, so the top of the shadow pile is always the current smallest.

**One line to remember:** Keep a second stack whose top always holds the minimum so far, pushing and popping it in lockstep with the main stack to get the minimum in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
A plain stack can push, pop, and read the top in constant time, but finding the minimum would normally require scanning every element, which is linear. The Min Stack trick removes that scan.

We keep two stacks. The main stack holds the actual values. The auxiliary minimum stack holds, at each position, the minimum of all elements from the bottom up to that point. When we push a value, we push it on the main stack, and we push onto the minimum stack the smaller of the new value and the current top of the minimum stack. If the minimum stack is empty, the new value becomes the first minimum.

When we pop, we pop both stacks together so they stay aligned. The top operation reads the main stack's top. The getMin operation reads the minimum stack's top, which by construction is always the smallest value currently present.

Because each operation is a handful of constant-time stack operations, every operation including getMin is O(1). The cost is O(n) extra space for the second stack. A space optimization is to push onto the minimum stack only when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum, and pop from it only when the popped value equals the current minimum, but the two-stack-in-lockstep version is simpler to reason about and still constant time.

A senior nuance: using "less than or equal" rather than "less than" in the optimized version matters for duplicates of the minimum; using strict "less than" would pop the minimum marker too early and report a wrong minimum. Another nuance is always pushing a mirror entry in the simple version so the two stacks never drift out of alignment.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's trading desk pushes and pops pending order amounts on a stack as orders are staged and cancelled. The risk monitor must, at any instant, know the smallest pending order amount still on the stack to check a floor rule, and it must get that answer instantly even as orders churn.

This is exactly how a Min Stack works. The minimum of the current stack is available in constant time.

Problem 2 — When the smallest order is cancelled (popped), the reported minimum must immediately reflect the next smallest still on the stack, with no rescan.

This is exactly why the auxiliary minimum stack is popped in lockstep, so its new top is instantly the correct new minimum.

The code will have a `MinStack` class backed by two `java.util.Deque` stacks, and a runnable demo that pushes several order amounts, reads the minimum, pops, and reads the minimum again with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a sequence of pushes and pops of order amounts.

Step 1: `push(50000)` puts 50000 on the main stack and 50000 on the minimum stack because the minimum stack was empty. The current minimum is 50000.

Step 2: `push(30000)` puts 30000 on the main stack. The smaller of 30000 and the current minimum 50000 is 30000, so 30000 is pushed on the minimum stack. The current minimum is 30000.

Step 3: `push(80000)` puts 80000 on the main stack. The smaller of 80000 and the current minimum 30000 is 30000, so 30000 is pushed again on the minimum stack. The current minimum stays 30000, and the top is 80000.

Step 4: `push(20000)` makes the minimum 20000. A `pop` then removes 20000 from both stacks, so the minimum stack's new top is 30000 again.

Step 5: Two more pops remove 80000 and 30000. After those pops the only remaining value is 50000, so the minimum stack's top, and therefore getMin, is 50000.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:00:00 INFO    top=80000 min=30000
2026-10-27 13:00:00 INFO    after push 20000 min=20000
2026-10-27 13:00:00 INFO    after pop min=30000
2026-10-27 13:00:00 INFO    after more pops min=50000
```

```
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + push(value): void                  │  O(1)
  │  + pop(): long                        │  O(1)
  │  + top(): long                        │  O(1)
  │  + getMin(): long                     │  O(1)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for pop():
    Pre:  stack non-empty (else IllegalStateException)
    Post: both stacks shrink by one, stay aligned; getMin reflects new top
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Min Stack is a stack that supports push, pop, and top in the usual way but adds a getMin operation that returns the smallest element currently in the stack, and the requirement is that all four operations run in constant time. A plain stack would have to scan every element to find the minimum, which is linear, so the trick is to maintain a second stack that tracks the minimum as the stack grows and shrinks.

The design keeps a main stack of the actual values and an auxiliary minimum stack. Each time I push a value, I also push onto the minimum stack the smaller of the new value and the current top of the minimum stack, so the top of the minimum stack is always the minimum of everything currently stored. When I pop, I pop both stacks together so they stay perfectly aligned, which means the moment the current minimum is removed, the new top of the minimum stack is instantly the next smallest value. The top operation reads the main stack and getMin reads the minimum stack.

Every operation is a constant number of simple stack operations, so getMin is constant time just like the rest, at the cost of linear extra space for the second stack. There is a space-optimized variant that only pushes onto the minimum stack when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum and only pops it when the popped value equals the current minimum, and the subtle point there is to use less than or equal rather than strict less than so that duplicate minimum values are tracked correctly.

In my project at National Bank of India, the trading desk staged and cancelled pending order amounts on a stack, and the risk monitor had to know the smallest pending amount at every instant to enforce a floor rule. The Min Stack gave that answer in constant time even as orders churned rapidly, and because the minimum stack was popped in lockstep with the main stack, cancelling the smallest order immediately surfaced the next smallest without any rescan.
